old: Customers sometimes arrived at local shops only to discover that the opening hours listed online were out of date. Shop owners decided to create one shared directory where each business could update its own details. They began by checking every listing and adding a simple form for reporting changes. During the school term, the group reviewed the information and asked customers whether the directory was easy to use. Fewer people arrived after a shop had closed, suggesting that the new system was useful. The owners still faced one problem: some businesses forgot to report holiday hours. They plan to send a monthly reminder and ask each shop to confirm its details before long weekends. The directory is practical because it gives customers current information without requiring a complicated new service.
new: Live-stream shopping has become a popular way for small sellers in Thailand to reach customers. Instead of posting photos and waiting for orders, sellers appear on camera, show their products, and answer viewers’ questions in real time. A clothing seller in Chiang Mai says her sales doubled after she began going live three evenings a week. However, the method is more demanding than it looks. Sellers must prepare products in advance, speak clearly for long periods, and respond quickly to comments. Some viewers also complain that the excitement of a live sale makes them buy things they do not really need. Consumer groups advise shoppers to check return policies before paying and to wait a few minutes before deciding. For sellers, experts suggest starting with short sessions and asking a friend to help read comments, so that the host can focus on presenting.

old: Items left in classrooms and public areas often remained unclaimed for weeks, so the student services office tried a more organized lost-property system. Staff recorded each item, assigned it a code, and posted a weekly list without including personal details. Found objects were kept in secure boxes until owners could describe them. Over six weeks, more students collected their belongings, and staff spent less time answering general inquiries. Privacy still mattered: valuable items required an identity check before they could be returned. The office plans to publish clear collection rules and review the process each term. The aim is to create a lasting system that is easy to use while protecting students' personal information.
new: Part-time library assistant wanted: Riverside Public Library is looking for a part-time assistant to work on Saturdays and two weekday evenings. Applicants should be at least eighteen, enjoy working with people, and feel comfortable using a computer catalog. Previous library experience is helpful but not required, as full training will be provided during the first month. The position pays 120 baht per hour, and staff may borrow up to fifteen items at a time. To apply, send a short letter explaining why you would like the job, together with the name of one person who can describe your work or study. Applications close on 30 April, and interviews will take place the following week.

old: Energy volunteers wanted to help families reduce unnecessary electricity use. They shared a short checklist and demonstrated how appliances can continue drawing power while in standby mode. Simple plug meters allowed volunteers to show the difference between switching a device off and leaving it on. Some households reduced avoidable electricity use, but the amount saved varied because homes had different appliances and routines. The volunteers asked families to compare their readings over a month and share the results. They plan to adjust the checklist so that it reflects the changes that were most useful in different homes. The project showed that practical energy advice should be based on measured results rather than general assumptions.
new: The City History Museum will close to the public from 1 June for eight months while workers repair its leaking roof and replace the old electrical system. During the closure, about two hundred objects will move to a temporary gallery in the central library, where entry will remain free. School groups that have already booked visits can choose a library tour or an online session with a museum educator. Some local cafés near the museum are worried about losing customers, and the city council has promised to review their situation in September. The museum expects to reopen in February with a new children’s room and longer weekend hours.
